articles.body: Published: 2026-11-20Description Description Severity Notes On November 18, 2026, F5 disclosed HTTP/2 vulnerabilities CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007 in NGINX Open Source (1.19.7-1.31.8 for CVE-2026-123633; 1.9.5-1.31.8 for CVE-2026-123007) and NGINX Plus, alongside eight additional NGINX CVEs in F5's master advisory (K000164058). Under specific configuration and traffic conditions, an unauthenticated remote attacker can crash an NGINX worker process (DoS) or potentially achieve remote code execution (RCE). Google Cloud's core load balancing and managed infrastructure (including Google Front End, Cloud Load Balancing, GKE control plane, Cloud Run, Cloud Functions, and App Engine) are not affected. This bulletin provides guidance for customers operating self-managed NGINX deployments on Google Cloud. What should I do? Managed Google Cloud services: No customer action is required if you rely solely on unaffected Google Cloud managed platforms (including Google Front End, Cloud Load Balancing, GKE control plane, Cloud Run, Cloud Functions, and App Engine). Google is patching any isolated Google-managed components internally, with zero customer impact and no customer action required. Customer-managed NGINX on Google Cloud (GKE Ingress Controllers, Compute Engine VMs, and NGINX-based Cloud Marketplace images): Google has also temporarily delisted affected Google-maintained Click-to-Deploy NGINX listings on Cloud Marketplace while patched images are being prepared. Patches for GKE 1.37 on Container-Optimized OS and Ubuntu node images are still in progress. A denial-of-service vulnerability (CVE-2026-99288) was discovered in the Linux kernel TCP implementation. The flaw can cause a kernel panic (denial of service) on the affected virtual machine; it does not allow privilege escalation or container breakout to code execution on the host. A remote attacker can trigger it by sending specially crafted TCP packets to a reachable TCP listener on a node, Pod, or the cluster control plane's IP-based endpoint. Internal traffic within the same VPC can also trigger this vulnerability. GKE Standard clusters and GKE Autopilot clusters running Container-Optimized OS or Ubuntu prior to the patched versions are affected across both cluster control planes and worker nodes. Under certain conditions, an attacker could infer data from the store queue or the L1 data cache, potentially leaking sensitive information across privilege boundaries. articles.body: Published: 2026-11-04Updated: 2026-11-18Description Description Severity Notes 2026-11-18 Update: Added patch versions for GKE. A vulnerability (CVE-2026-98432) was discovered in the Linux kernel IPv4 TCP stack. The flaw can cause a kernel panic or a container escape (root code execution on the node). An unprivileged process in a container can trigger it locally, without special capabilities such as CAP_NET_RAW. A network attacker can also trigger it by sending TCP packets with IPv4 options to a listener on the node or on the cluster control plane. The network attack requires access to a TCP listener on your nodes, Pods, or the control plane's IP-based endpoint. Clusters that restrict this access to trusted sources, for example with firewall rules and control plane authorized networks, are not exposed to network attacks. GKE Standard clusters and GKE Autopilot clusters are impacted. For instructions and more details, see the GKE security bulletin. Medium CVE-2026-98432

articles.body: Published: 2026-11-02Description Description Severity Notes On Saturday, October 17, 2026, Google received a report from a security researcher regarding the compromise of private keys associated with eight eMudhra subordinate Certification Authority (CA) certificates, including those cross-signed by AAA Certificate Services. Consequently, these CA certificates are no longer trusted and are being revoked. Google Cloud infrastructure has not been breached. Security telemetry shows no evidence of exploitation against Google Cloud workloads. Applications built with the Google Cloud SDK Libraries are affected if their TLS trust store still accepts emSign ECC Root CA - G3, emSign Root TLS CA - G3, or AAA Certificate Services. The Google Cloud SDK Libraries themselves don't bundle CA certificates, with one exception: Java's com.google.api-client:google-api-client before 2.9.2. In all other cases, the trust store comes from a transport dependency (including the Google-maintained gRPC packages), the language runtime, or the operating system, so the fix is an update to those rather than to the Google Cloud SDK Libraries. In Java, Ruby, and PHP, upgrading the Google client libraries also pulls the fix in. The sections below give the action for each language. What should I do? Find your language below and apply the recommended actions. Then rebuild and redeploy your container images. Python The following packages are affected: certifi earlier than 2026.10.19 (REST transports). httplib2 earlier than 0.32.1, used by google-api-python-client and google-auth-httplib2; its bundled trust store is used when certifi is not installed. grpcio earlier than 1.84.1 (gRPC transports); bundled root store, does not read the operating system trust store. You can take the following actions to resolve these issues: Upgrade certifi to 2026.10.19 or later. Upgrade httplib2 to 0.32.1 or later. Upgrade grpcio to 1.84.1 or later. Patch releases for earlier release lines are being published; see GHSA-2xm2-c8xx-p9vh for the current list of fixed versions. Advisories: GHSA-6q48-6c7w-9gw2 (certifi), GHSA-2xm2-c8xx-p9vh (grpcio). Java The following packages and trust stores are affected: com.google.api-client:google-api-client earlier than 2.9.2, when the HTTP transport is created with GoogleNetHttpTransport.newTrustedTransport(). Versions earlier than 2.9.0 always use a bundled trust store that includes AAA Certificate Services; versions 2.9.0 and 2.9.1 use it when the Java Development Kit...

articles.body: Published: 2026-10-21Updated: 2026-10-28Description Description Severity Notes 2026-10-28 Update: For Cloud Run, Cloud Run functions, and Google App Engine Standard, all supported versions of PHP 8.2 and later are patched. Take immediate protective action by redeploying your resources with updated dependencies. Two remote code execution vulnerabilities were found in the open-source PHP language. While Google Cloud itself is not vulnerable, users of this language running on Google Cloud may be vulnerable. The following language versions are affected by this vulnerability: All PHP versions between 5.4 and 8.5 The following framework versions include fixes for this vulnerability: PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 What should I do? Customers should take immediate action to protect their workloads by redeploying their workloads with updated dependencies. articles.body: Updated November 23, 2026: Bring Your Own Telephony (BYOT) is now generally available. We've updated this post with BYOT details.Updated October 30, 2026: We have updated this post with additional information as the feature is now generally available. Thank you for your patience. [What and why]Choose Your Own Telephony Provider (CYOT) and Bring Your Own Telephony Provider (BYOT) are now generally available in Microsoft Entra ID. Both connect Microsoft Entra to a telephony provider through an integration in your Azure subscription, but you purchase and deploy them differently. Microsoft Entra continues to manage the authentication experience, including one-time passcode (OTP) generation and validation, and your provider delivers the SMS messages and voice calls. CYOT is the recommended option when a supported offering meets your coverage, contractual and compliance requirements. It gives you providers evaluated by Microsoft for geographic coverage and fraud protection, purchasing through Microsoft Security Store, billing through your Azure subscription and guided deployment in the Microsoft Entra admin center. BYOT is for cases where an existing provider agreement or a specific requirement can't be met by the supported CYOT offerings. You get your provider's ready-to-deploy integration package, set up your account directly with the provider, and configure the integration through APIs. With either option, your organization owns the Azure resources in your subscription and your telephony provider account. Microsoft-provided SMS and voice authentication starts retiring on February 1, 2027. If your users need SMS or voice after that date, set up CYOT or BYOT before then. Microsoft recommends phishing-resistant authentication methods, such as passkeys, instead of SMS or voice. Use a telephony provider only for user groups that have a business, regulatory or technical need for telephony-based authentication.[What you need to do]If your organization needs to keep SMS or voice authentication: Identify users who need SMS or voice. Confirm which users have a requirement that phishing-resistant methods can't meet. Choose your option and provider. Review CYOT and BYOT. Use CYOT when a supported provider meets your coverage, contractual and compliance requirements. Otherwise, use BYOT. Check prerequisites. You need an Azure subscription with a valid payment method to host the integration, plus the Owner role or Contributor plus Role Based Access Control Administrator. For CYOT, the subscription must also be eligible for Security Store purchases. Estimate costs. Review provider pricing and Azure hosting costs. Set up and roll out. Follow the setup guide for CYOT or BYOT. Start in evaluation mode, then move traffic to your provider in stages. Complete your transition before February 1, 2027. articles.body: CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2024-10441 Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM) Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output Vulnerability CVE-2026-40217 BerriAI LiteLLM Unprotected Alternate Channel Vulnerability CVE-2026-90436 Apache Axis Unsafe Reflection Vulnerability CVE-2026-90817 Vanderbilt University Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) Code Injection Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

articles.author: yuvalpery
articles.body: Introduction On November 17, 2026, CVE-2026-114938, also known as Java4Shell, a critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability affecting OpenJDK, was publicly disclosed. Under specific conditions, specially crafted Base64 input can trigger memory corruption in affected Java runtimes, potentially allowing unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code. We strongly recommend that customers update the Java runtime used by their own applications to a patched version or update third-party Java-based applications to a version that includes the security fix, as applicable. Updating the affected Java runtime is the primary way to fully remediate this vulnerability. For further details, refer to Oracle's official security advisory. Azure Web Application Firewall (WAF) has developed mitigations designed to detect and block known HTTP-based exploitation patterns associated with this vulnerability, providing an additional layer of protection while customers apply the necessary security updates. These mitigations are intended to complement patching, not replace it. About CVE-2026-114938 CVE-2026-114938 is a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder. When an affected Java application processes specially crafted Base64 input, the vulnerability can cause heap memory corruption, potentially leading to application crashes, sensitive information disclosure, or remote code execution. The vulnerability primarily affects unpatched OpenJDK-based Java runtimes version 17.0.6 and later, including Java 21, 25, and 27, running on x86-64 processors supporting the AVX-512 VBMI instruction set. Exploitation requires attacker-controlled input to reach the vulnerable Base64 decoding functionality. ARM64 systems and x86-64 processors without AVX-512 VBMI support are not known to be affected. Recommended action: Update affected Java runtimes and third-party Java-based applications to versions containing the security fix as soon as possible. articles.body: As more work happens in the browser, the browser has become a prime target for attackers. A fake CAPTCHA or a convincing error message persuades users to take an action that seems harmless, like running a command or approving a request. In these attacks, the user unknowingly carries the threat from the browser to the operating system. Once that happens, the attacker can install malware, steal credentials, or establish a foothold on the device. This sequence creates a practical challenge for defenders. Preventing breach at the time of execution is key, and at the same time security teams need confidence that protection is deployed, communicating, current, and functioning across all endpoints in the environment. At Microsoft Ignite 2026, Microsoft Defender is introducing protection designed to block some of the most prevalent browser-based attacks, and new capabilities to better and more easily manage the endpoint estate itself. Together, these updates connect two responsibilities that security teams often manage separately: stopping an attack when it becomes executable and continuously verifying that the protection layer is ready to respond. Protect against browser-based ClickFix attacks Today’s attacks often begin with a lure in the browser that leads to an attack on the endpoint. articles.author: Alon Rosental
articles.body: AI has accelerated vulnerability discovery for defenders and attackers alike. An attacker can now turn a vulnerability into a working exploit within hours, but patching can’t keep pace. Our data shows that 38% of critical Patch Tuesday exposures remain unpatched for more than five days, and attackers operate in the gap between exposure and remediation. To keep up, organizations need protection that moves as fast as critical vulnerabilities are discovered, without forcing rushed patches or disrupting the business. That’s why today we’re excited to introduce vulnerability shielding in Microsoft Defender, in preview: Vulnerability shielding applies targeted, temporary protection to vulnerable systems in the gap between exposure and remediation, buying defenders time before they can apply a permanent patch. This AI-based capability reasons over the latest threat intelligence and each organization’s unique environment to choose the narrowest effective protection. Vulnerability shielding operates at two critical moments: Proactively limit exposure: The Risk Reduction Agent in Microsoft Perception as part of the Reduce exposure risk playbook creates a tailored plan for shielding vulnerabilities when patching is not immediately available or possible. Shields are time bound, reversible, choose the path of minimal business disruption, and retire automatically once the patch lands. Nothing is implemented without your approval. Protect during an active attack: When attack disruption in Microsoft Defender identifies an ongoing attack, it autonomously applies vulnerability shielding controls to exposed assets, cutting off new attack paths for adversaries and limiting the impact to your organization. Vulnerability shielding does not replace patching. Patching is the fix; shielding is designed to protect the interim risk. Autonomous protection enabled by a modern cyber stack Microsoft's cyber stack connects context, agentic reasoning, and native enforcement in a continuous loop. That integration enables vulnerability shielding to move from exposure insight to targeted protection at the speed an attack demands. Signals and context: Vulnerability shielding builds a deep, continuously updated exposure map of your environment across assets, identities, vulnerabilities, attack paths, and business context. articles.title: The risks of device code authentication for AI coding agents
articles.summary: Lab research shows how device code phishing, a technique that applies to any device-flow client, can extend to AI coding agents, using GitHub Copilot CLI as an illustrative example. The post The risks of device code authentication for AI coding agents appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog.
articles.author: Microsoft Security Research
articles.body: In this article From a familiar phishing technique to an AI coding agentHow the attack worksOne approval, four ways the impact can spreadTurning a phishing attempt into a Defender signalMitigation and protection guidanceReferencesLearn More Device code phishing has become a recurring route to account takeover. Instead of stealing a password, an attacker persuades someone to approve a sign-in on a legitimate site simply by entering a code. The resulting access often can reach email, files, or other cloud services, depending on the account and the permissions granted. Notable earlier campaigns such as EvilTokens show how readily this technique can be scaled to do real damage. Microsoft worked hard with partners in industry and law enforcement to disrupt EvilTokens in September 2026. That led us to a different question: what else can an attacker do with a phished device code authorization? What happens when the same trick targets an AI agent rather than a mailbox? We used GitHub Copilot CLI as an illustrative example. Depending on its configuration, it can work with code, run commands on a user’s machine, retain context across sessions, and allow an active session to be steered remotely. Like many command-line tools, it supports the OAuth device flow for sign-in. The phishing technique itself is not specific to GitHub or Copilot CLI: any public client that supports the device flow can be abused the same way, and the attacker chooses the requested scopes when starting the flow. We explored this scenario in a controlled lab simulation. A victim test account approved a GitHub device-code request initiated by an attacker client we controlled. With that approval, we were able to analyze four possible outcomes: Steer an active Copilot CLI session remotely, if the user has enabled remote control and organization policy allows it, and, subject to local permissions and approval settings, have the agent run commands on the user’s machine. Add misleading entries to the agent’s memory that could influence later interactions. Read Copilot CLI sessions that were synchronized to the cloud. Access private repositories available to the affected account. These are proof-of-concept results showing how existing features, working as designed, could be abused after a phished authorization; they are not attacks we have observed in the wild. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? articles.author: CISA
articles.body: Purpose CISA strongly urges organizations to immediately patch the recently disclosed Oracle Java vulnerability CVE-2026-114938. This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as “Java4Shell,” affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK). Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM and allow for unauthenticated remote code execution. Actions to take CISA urges organizations to take the following actions: Identify affected Java installations. Review your software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party applications or included in container images and appliances. Note: JDKs and Java runtimes may not appear as separate entries in software inventories. Apply relevant Java and vendor patches as soon as they are available, prioritizing internet-facing systems. If immediate patching is not feasible, implement temporary compensating controls, such as restricting and validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits, and limiting unauthenticated access. Review Oracle’s security advisory for guidance on patching and affected products and versions. Monitor for indicators of suspicious activity, including rogue runtimes, unexpected JVM crashes, and suspicious Java processes. articles.body: In this article Phishing attack overviewAttack chain overviewMitigation and protection guidanceReferencesLearn More On November 13, 2026, Microsoft Threat Intelligence observed a coordinated, high-volume phishing campaign targeting organizations across multiple sectors worldwide. The threat actors used phishing emails disguised as legitimate Microsoft 365 service-health notifications to lure recipients into clicking a malicious link. The messages created a false sense of urgency by claiming that emails had been held during a service disruption and would be deleted within 24 hours unless the recipient took action to restore them. This is consistent with historical attacker campaigns which continuously look for notable global events to exploit in their social engineering lures. Microsoft identified the threat actor’s use of specific sender domain names, randomized outage subjects, recipient-specific tracking links, and a common non-Microsoft destination to make the messages appear relevant while complicating simple pattern matching. Multiple threat actors may continue to look for ways to exploit notable global events in any social engineering pretext. If credentials were entered, organizations should consider the risk of account compromise, mailbox access, business email compromise, internal phishing, inbox-rule manipulation, and access to cloud collaboration data. Microsoft Defender blocks malicious domains used in this campaign, and Microsoft Defender for Office 365 blocks and quarantines phishing emails. We will continue to monitor this campaign and other related threats. articles.body: Introduction Azure DDoS Protection now covers the public IP addresses used by Azure NAT Gateway StandardV2, in public preview. Customers can protect the StandardV2 IPv4 and IPv6 public IPs that carry their outbound internet traffic from network-layer DDoS attacks, using the same DDoS Network Protection and IP Protection they already use. There's no new API, feature registration or appliance to manage, and DDoS protection doesn't open the gateway to unsolicited inbound connections. Why it matters NAT Gateway doesn't accept inbound connections, but its public IPs are still reachable from the internet, and they're the identity of everything behind them. Your outbound IPs are known to others. Every external service your workloads call sees these IPs. Partners, SaaS providers and banks often keep them on allow-lists. Anyone who learns them can aim traffic at them. One IP set serves many workloads. Every VM in the associated subnets shares the gateway's public IPs. A flood that saturates these IPs can disrupt outbound connectivity for all of them at once. That includes calls to external APIs, partner integrations, package and update downloads, and telemetry. Outbound failures hurt production. An attack on the NAT IPs doesn't have to reach your workloads to cause an outage. It only has to break their path to the internet. Same protection as your inbound endpoints. Until now, customers could protect inbound public IPs but not the IPs behind NAT Gateway StandardV2. With this preview, outbound IPs get automatic network-layer mitigation, plus the DDoS metrics, diagnostics and alerts they already use. Easier compliance. Security policies and posture checks that require DDoS protection on all public IPs no longer have an exception for NAT Gateway IPs. articles.author: Jdasari
articles.body: More control, broader coverage with Azure DDoS Protection custom policy Fine-tune protocol-specific DDoS detection for internet-facing workloads while keeping Azure’s adaptive protection as the default. Organizations depend on Azure DDoS Protection to monitor traffic continuously and mitigate network-layer attacks at cloud scale. Most workloads benefit from a hands-off, adaptive experience. But applications with planned traffic surges, unusual packet-rate patterns, strict latency requirements, or distinct environments sometimes need more control over when mitigation begins. Azure DDoS Protection custom policy adds that optional control. It lets you define fixed inbound detection thresholds for TCP, UDP, and TCP SYN traffic and apply them to supported public endpoints. The result is a protection model that remains automatic by default while giving application and network teams a precise override when their workload calls for it. In one sentence: Custom policy extends Azure DDoS Protection’s adaptive baseline with optional, protocol-specific controls; it does not replace the turnkey default. Azure DDoS Protection custom policy is now generally available, letting customers replace machine-learning auto-tuning with fixed protocol-specific detection thresholds per protected resource across Azure resource types with public IPs. Available on Network Protection and IP Protection SKUs, it already covers 929 policies and about 1,970 attachments pre-GA, led by OpenAI. Why customers asked for more control Adaptive auto-tuning works well for most workloads because Azure learns the normal traffic profile of each protected endpoint and adjusts mitigation thresholds as that profile changes. A fixed, application-specific threshold can be useful when traffic is predictable in a way that the service cannot infer ahead of time. A gaming launch, ticket sale, live stream, or seasonal event is expected to create a sudden but legitimate increase in packet rate. A high-throughput service regularly operates near a threshold and needs an explicitly controlled trigger. A latency-sensitive workload benefits from a tighter mitigation threshold for one protocol. Development, test, and production environments need separate policies and change controls. Security teams want repeatable, infrastructure-as-code deployment and verifiable associations to protected endpoints. articles.title: Protecting Microsoft's SAP workload with Microsoft Sentinel for SAP: the RISE with SAP chapter
articles.summary: Inside Track | Microsoft Digital When infrastructure operations shift, security visibility must evolve with the operating model Four years ago, we told the story of how Microsoft became Customer Zero for using Microsoft Sentinel as the SIEM for its own SAP estate, pairing a then-new product...
articles.author: MartinPankraz
articles.body: Inside Track | Microsoft Digital When infrastructure operations shift, security visibility must evolve with the operating model Four years ago, we told the story of how Microsoft became Customer Zero for using Microsoft Sentinel as the SIEM for its own SAP estate, pairing a then-new product “Sentinel Solution for SAP” with our existing SOAR platform and proving out cross-correlation between SAP and the rest of the enterprise. The ambition was stated plainly at the time: an internally managed and configured SIEM that could baseline user behaviors and detect anomalies across SAP, spanning the OS and network layer, the database layer, and the application and business logic layers. Then we moved to RISE with SAP on Azure. With that move, responsibility for instrumenting one of those layers transitioned to SAP under the RISE operating model. The visibility challenge shared responsibility creates In RISE with SAP, SAP operates the underlying infrastructure, operating system, and database as part of the managed service. This changes how customers obtain security telemetry from those layers and raises an important shared-responsibility question: how can the customer SOC maintain end-to-end visibility while SAP operates the platform? The layers remain relevant to security monitoring, so visibility must extend across both SAP-managed and customer-managed parts of the landscape. What changed: SAP LogServ meets Sentinel for SAP SAP LogServ is SAP's centralized log service for RISE-managed landscapes, carrying the security-relevant telemetry from the layers SAP now operates. Microsoft Sentinel for SAP ingests it directly, authenticated with managed identity for Azure. There is no stored secret, no rotation calendar and no bespoke connector for a future engineer to inherit and maintain. articles.author: RyadB
articles.body: The situation is familiar. One query spills to disk, tempdb grows until the volume fills and every other session on the instance starts failing. The engine has a lever for this since 2008: Resource Governor But for years years it was only available in Enterprise edition. If you were running Standard the only solution was monitoring alert. SQL Server 2025 changed that. Resource Governor is now available in Standard (and Standard Developer) edition and a new workload group setting caps how much tempdb data space a group of sessions can consume. However, there is a catch you should know before starting. On a default instance, the percentage form of the limit is stored but never enforced (even Reconfigure succeed), just a warning in the error log. Good to know What changed Two separate changes landed. Resource Governor moved down the edition ladder. This is now available in Enterprise, Enterprise Developer, Standard and Standard Developer. But tempdb space resource governance is new. Two new arguments on CREATE WORKLOAD GROUP and ALTER WORKLOAD GROUP, GROUP_MAX_TEMPDB_DATA_MB and GROUP_MAX_TEMPDB_DATA_PERCENT allow to cap the total tempdb data space consumed by all sessions in that group. How the limit behaves It is cumulative per group, not per request. The documentation is precise "The limit is for the total space consumed in tempdb by all sessions in a workload group." A session behaving correctly can be aborted because other sessions in its group already spent the budget. That is the intended design, you are protecting the instance not limiting individual queries. Enforcement is an abort, not a throttle. A request that would push the group over its limit aborts with error 1138, severity 17: Could not allocate a new page for database 'tempdb' because that would exceed the limit set for workload group <groupName> Accounting is in 8 KB pages. A page holding 1 row still costs 8 KB. Space is charged for temporary tables, table variables, table-valued parameters, cursors, non-temporary tables created in tempdb and structures such as spools, spills, worktables and workfiles. Another good thing to know: for global temporary tables and regular tables in tempdb, space is charged to the workload group that inserted the first row even if sessions in other groups add, modify or remove rows afterwards. If the group is dropped while the table still exists then the space stops being charged to anyone. Governance applies to tempdb data files only, not the transaction log....

articles.summary: Microsoft Defender Research and the AI Red Team discuss how poisoned datasets and poisoned model checkpoints can trigger remote code execution and other malicious activities. articles.author: Giorgio Severi
articles.body: In this article Dataset poisoning: Teaching agents to discover and misuse toolsModel poisoning: Building reliable backdoors that persist and transferWhat the studies show about agent backdoorsMitigation and protection guidanceSecuring agents beyond the modelReferences Learn More As organizations increasingly deploy specialized AI agents, trust cannot depend solely on a model behaving as expected during evaluation or normal use. As Satya Nadella has argued in Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era, trustworthy enterprise AI requires independent observability and controls that sit outside the model. Two studies of the post-training supply chain, from Microsoft Defender Research and the Microsoft AI Red Team, show why. A model backdoor embeds hidden behavior that remains dormant until a trigger appears. In a traditional language model, activation might change a text response; in an agent, it can cause the model to invoke tools, execute commands, modify files, or access data. The two studies examine attacks with different levels of access. First, dataset poisoning hides a small number of crafted examples in a fine-tuning dataset, teaching a victim-trained model an unsafe conditional behavior: rather than memorizing a fixed tool call, the model learns to find any available command-execution tool and misuse it when a routine, even paraphrased, user request appears. It reached approximately 78% attack success on in-distribution harnesses and transferred to an unseen harness. Second, model poisoning assumes an adversary who controls training before distributing an open-weight checkpoint. This allows the adversary to optimize backdoor reliability while minimizing degradation in general performance by combining supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with reinforcement learning (RL). In this setting, average success on unseen repositories reached 84.1% to 94.8%, with additional transfer across coding harnesses. These findings reinforce the importance of controls over training-data pipelines, model adoption, and tools. Introduction Coding and terminal agents do more than generate text. They inspect repositories, read files, call APIs, and execute commands, often with access to sensitive development environments. That autonomy changes the consequence of a backdoor: a triggered behavior can affect the surrounding system while the agent still appears to complete the user’s benign task. articles.body: In this article When one RCE stops being just one RCEObserved attack chainsHow threat actors deploy and operate GSocketHow GSocket reconnects without a fixed C2 addressMitigation and protection guidanceReferencesLearn More Microsoft observed multiple incidents in which threat actors deployed GSocket, an open source remote access tool, on compromised Linux servers. Threat actors used Gsocket to maintain access even after the vulnerabilities used for initial compromise were remediated. This turned a single web application compromise into persistent access that outlasted the remediation of the original vulnerabilities. Defenders investigating affected hosts should look for evidence of GSocket deployment, persistence, privilege escalation, and outbound connections, rather than treating application patching alone as complete remediation. Microsoft Defender for Endpoint telemetry shows this activity growing over recent months and concentrated on web applications and hosting environments. GSocket relays traffic through a shared public network, so there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block. When one RCE stops being just one RCE Exploiting a web application vulnerability gives a threat actor command execution in the context of the web server process. That access lasts only while the vulnerability remains unpatched and the service keeps running. Patching the application or restarting the service can remove it. To keep access, threat actors typically add a persistence mechanism, and each common option has drawbacks. SSH keys added to authorized_keys are easy for administrators to find during an audit. Reverse shells depend on threat actor-controlled servers that defenders can block or sinkhole. Custom implants require ongoing development and maintenance. The same trade-offs apply when initial access comes through remote access services or cloud shell sessions. GSocket addresses these drawbacks, which helps explain why multiple unrelated threat actors have adopted it. Shared relay infrastructure. Traffic passes through the Global Socket Relay Network, a public relay service. The threat actor does not register or host any infrastructure, so there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block. Organizations can still restrict access to the relay itself. One full-time researcher and one intern led this three-month effort, which has so far produced 59 public upstream reports and 33 assigned CVEs. We confirmed working root privilege-escalation exploits for eight of those CVEs, and fixes for 38 of our reports have been merged into mainline. Finding the bugs was only part of the work. The initial scans produced 26,502 raw findings in about two weeks, but turning those results into reproducible bugs, upstream reports, and patches took months of expert investigation and collaboration with Linux maintainers. In this post, we look back at how we went from thousands of potential findings to validated vulnerabilities and upstream fixes, and what we learned about scaling vulnerability discovery with AI. From scans to reports We focused on several core kernel subsystems, such as networking, filesystems, and security modules. Our selection criteria were straightforward: we picked security-sensitive components with no obvious dependence on specialized hardware, making QEMU-based validation simple and unified. articles.summary: Microsoft Research has released new threat research detailing how a capable agent model could be turned into a sleeper agent by editing fewer than ten neurons to inject a short payload; Microsoft Research has also found that this threat is detectable by frontier agents, which can identify anomalous...
articles.author: Microsoft Threat Intelligence
articles.body: Microsoft Research has released new threat research detailing how a capable agent model could be turned into a sleeper agent by editing fewer than 10 neurons to inject a short payload. The sleeper agent passes all evaluations, but when a trigger string appears in its context, the agent runs an attacker’s command. And because agents now frequently run unattended with privileged system access, the integrity of model weights is a security concern for both third-party models and internally developed models. Key findings from Microsoft Research include: Software abuse and manipulation are familiar threats. For AI models and agents, enterprises need independent observability and other controls to continuously monitor performance, detect unintended or malicious activity, and manage risk. Satya Nadella recently outlined this approach in a blog post. A backdoored model can pass evaluations. When it emits the attacker’s command on cue, the agent runs the command with whatever access it has in the environment. The attack needs inference-only compute. If a machine has enough RAM to run a model, it has enough resources to weight-space backdoor it. Claude Code with Opus 4.5 discovered most of this threat autonomously. Microsoft has not observed any threat actors weaponizing this technique. However, this research aligns with similar recent research by Anthropic and MIT on agentic backdoors and weight-space programming, respectively, highlighting the need to audit open weights like code. Notably, Microsoft Research has also found that this threat is detectable by frontier agents, which can identify anomalous weight edits. Using frontier agents as auditors can help automate the defense against this threat. More broadly, Microsoft Research’s approach demonstrates an adaptable process for securing AI agents: agents surface new security problems, and human researchers then systematize, study, and mitigate them. Learn more from the Microsoft Research Blog: Lazare, veni foras: Reprogramming dormant neurons to backdoor AI agents Mitigation and protection guidance Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to defend against this threat as part of a broader defense-in-depth approach. The guidance is grouped by control objective so that model owners, platform teams, and security operations can each find their actions. Audit model weights before deployment and after every update Diff every checkpoint against its declared base model before deployment and after each update....

articles.body: In this article How we found and validated the bugsPattern 1: Trusting code not to panicPattern 2: Trusting user-provided implementations to be correctPattern 3: Trusting the underlying systemWhy Rust still matters and advancing vulnerability discovery with AIRust's high bar is hard to meet but worth keeping Microsoft’s FORGE Lab found several memory safety issues in Rust’s standard library (std and core), including cases where code written entirely in safe Rust can trigger undefined behavior. The research used Hyenas, FORGE’s frontier research version of codename MDASH, an AI-powered vulnerability-scanning system. The findings reveal three recurring patterns of misplaced trust in unsafe code: trusting code not to panic, trusting user-provided implementations to be correct, and trusting the underlying system. Rust’s safety guarantees are precisely what make these findings interesting. Its rich type system and ownership model rule out whole classes of memory-safety issues, but much of the standard library relies on unsafe code underneath its safe APIs. When that code breaks its safety contract, even safe Rust can encounter behavior the language is designed to prevent. Rust’s memory-safety guarantees are increasingly important as the language becomes part of software that billions of people rely on every day. Billions of people are estimated to interact with Rust-based software or operating systems daily, often without knowing it. Microsoft made Rust a Tier-1 internal language alongside C++, C#, and TypeScript, GitHub rewrote the Copilot agent runtime in Rust, and Bun, Android, the Linux kernel, and Cloudflare are moving code to it as well. Much of this software relies on Rust’s foundational libraries, core and std, and the safety guarantees of the APIs they provide. Bugs in those libraries can have consequences well beyond the code where they originate. Unsafe Rust has been a long-running interest for us. Our team includes the people behind Rudra, a static analyzer that looked for memory-safety bugs across the Rust ecosystem in 2021. We also write many of our own tools in Rust, so its safety is more than a research topic for us. This year, we took a closer look at the standard library to see what kinds of mistakes still show up in its unsafe code today. articles.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence observed a sharp rise in email-based phishing activity at the end of Q3 2026 (July – September), even as QR code phishing declined, CAPTCHA-gated phishing recovered, and malicious messages spoofing familiar business-service sender domains exposed risks associated with...
articles.author: Microsoft Defender Security Research Team
articles.body: In this article Spoofed sender domainsQR code phishing attacksCAPTCHA-gated phishing tacticsMalicious payloadsBusiness contact impersonationMicrosoft Teams threatsNotable phishing campaignsDefending against email and collaboration threatsHunting queriesIndicators of compromise (IOCs) Microsoft Threat Intelligence detected approximately 7.3 billion email-based phishing threats from July through September, including a sharp increase to nearly 3 billion in September alone, up 41% from August. Yet the increase did not extend across the techniques that had driven threat actor activity earlier in the year. QR code phishing remained far below its early-year peak, while CAPTCHA-gated phishing reversed several months of decline, driven in part by renewed use of SVG attachments. Q2 in review Shifting tactics and other trends › Figure 1. Monthly detected email threat volume (January – September 2026) The quarter also highlighted how sender identity and security exceptions can shape the outcome of detected threats. Microsoft detected approximately 129 million malicious messages spoofing the sender domains of tracked business services. Many were delivered because organization- or user-configured exceptions overrode security protections, even after the messages failed authentication checks and were identified as malicious, showing how overly broad exceptions intended to preserve legitimate workflows can also expose them to impersonation. articles.body: Written in collaboration with yuvalpery​ and Gunjan Jain​ Introduction Today, two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities were disclosed in PHP. We strongly recommend that customers upgrade to a patched version of PHP as soon as possible. Upgrading is the only way to fully remediate these vulnerabilities. Read more on the PHP official website. Microsoft has been part of the coordinated industry response to these vulnerabilities, working alongside the PHP Foundation, Wiz, security researchers, and other industry partners to help protect customers. Azure Web Application Firewall (WAF) has developed mitigations against known exploitation patterns to provide an additional layer of protection while customers apply the PHP security updates. These protections are intended to complement patching and are not a replacement for it. About the vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-109618 - RCE via OOM corruption CVE-2026-109619- RCE via stale global state Both vulnerabilities can be exploited over the network without privileges or user interaction, with a high potential impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability. The vulnerabilities relate to PHP handling of memory when a request terminates abnormally, for example due to memory exhaustion or a fatal error. Under certain conditions, improper memory handling could allow an attacker to achieve remote code execution. Fixed versions: 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, 8.2.35. Refer to vendor guidancefor patching of different versions of PHP. Recommended action: upgrade PHP We recommend that customers: Upgrade all PHP deployments to a patched version, including virtual machines, containers, base images, and platform runtimes. articles.author: Jiacen Xu
articles.body: In this article Attack chain overviewMitigation and protection guidanceLearn More Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified an evolving fake-download campaign targeting users searching for cracked commercial software, free games, activators, plugins, and unofficial utilities. The campaign uses trojanized Inno Setup-style installers to distribute multiple monetized software payloads, referred to by the delivery system as “offers”, during a single installation session. Our investigation found that the installers use a per-offer callback and status-tracking model to manage delivery and record installation outcomes. We confirmed three downstream monetization branches that transformed affected devices into monetized assets, including by routing third-party internet traffic through the device, enrolling it in a distributed-computing platform, or installing additional utility-style software, often without users’ informed knowledge or consent. These products and components may have legitimate uses, but their silent installation through deceptive software bundles without informed user consent introduces security and privacy risks. Organizations can reduce their exposure to this activity by preventing the use of untrusted software sources, enabling potentially unwanted application protection, and monitoring for unexpected software installations and persistence mechanisms. This blog details the campaign’s execution model and confirmed outcomes and provides mitigation guidance, Microsoft Defender protection information, advanced hunting queries, MITRE ATT&CK mappings, and indicators of compromise to help defenders identify, investigate, and respond to related activity. articles.author: yuvalpery
articles.body: Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 contain a buffer overflow vulnerability in the Brotli decoder, according to the recently published CVE-2026-111497. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted Brotli-compressed stream to corrupt decoder memory, expose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially run arbitrary code. Any application that decompresses untrusted Brotli data may be affected. This includes Node.js and Python applications that bundle the vulnerable decoder, and services that accept request bodies with the Content-Encoding: br header. We strongly recommend upgrading Brotli to a patched version: 1.0.10, 1.1.1 or 1.2.1 (Brotli releases). If you use Node.js, upgrade to 22.23.4, 24.22.1 or 26.12.1 (Node.js security release). If you can't patch your applications right away, Azure WAF on Application Gateway, Application Gateway for Containers and Azure Front Door can help mitigate the inbound attack vector, which is Brotli-compressed request bodies sent to your application. Note: Azure WAF inspects only inbound requests to your application. It can't protect applications that fetch and decompress Brotli-encoded responses from external servers. Those applications must be patched. Built-in protection enabled by default If you use Azure WAF with DRS 2.2 on Application Gateway or Azure Front Door Premium, you're protected by default against crafted Brotli-compressed request bodies. Rule 920450 (Paranoia Level 1, enabled by default) checks requests against a list of restricted headers, and DRS 2.2 adds Content-Encoding to that list. The rule has a critical anomaly score, so a single match blocks the request when the WAF policy is in Prevention mode. Earlier rule set versions don't restrict the Content-Encoding header. If you're still on DRS 2.1, CRS 3.2 or earlier, we recommend upgrading to DRS 2.2 to get the latest protection. To learn how, see Upgrade CRS or DRS ruleset version. If your application uses Next.js image optimization, apply the BlockNextImageCVE2026111497 custom rule below, even if you're on DRS 2.2. Custom rules to mitigate CVE-2026-111497 The custom rules block two attack vectors: 1. CVE2026111497 blocks any request whose Content-Encoding header includes the br (Brotli) coding, which this attack uses. DRS 2.2 already covers this vector through rule 920450. articles.author: MaximeBombardier
articles.body: In April, I published a set of referential architecture diagrams for Microsoft Purview — Microsoft Purview Referential Architecture Diagrams. They have been useful in workshops and training sessions for a simple reason: one picture is worth a thousand words - attempting to explain the complex in a single image. Today I'm publishing an update focused on classification and labeling — and on the wave of public previews that make auto-labeling something you can scale across the entire estate with ease. ➡️ Download the interactive architecture on GitHub here. It's a self-contained HTML file - and it's a lot more than this picture! Why now: auto-labeling scales to the whole estate The most consequential change is surprisingly small. An auto-labeling policy can now be kept on while you edit it, without re-triggering simulation. Anyone who has run auto-labeling at scale knows why that matters. Until now, tuning a policy meant turning enforcement off, re-simulating, waiting, and turning it back on — delays every time you refined a rule. That friction made it challenging for organizations from broadening scope as fast as they wanted to. Removing it changes the operating model: you can simulate once with your conditions and expand scope (sites) when you're ready, without hitting the simulation limit. It arrives alongside a set of previews that lift every ceiling that used to cap the motion: Capacity is up 5x. Auto-labeling for SharePoint and OneDrive moves from 100,000 to up to 500,000 files per tenant per day (Roadmap ID 567890). Simulation goes from 4M to 20M items, so you can model against a real estate rather than a sample. Policy scope gets much bigger. Select up to 1,000 individual SharePoint sites per policy, adaptive scopes support up to 50,000 sites, and you can filter sites by the SiteTemplate property when configuring a policy (Roadmap ID 570445, MC1469958). Reporting finally tells you what happened. Audit and reporting now summarize the sensitive information types detected when labels are applied, and a new 30-day chart shows files processed per day so you can watch policy throughput. A per-policy coverage report correlates files processed during enforcement to the latest simulation run — including the files that enforcement processed but simulation never saw (Roadmap ID 568935). articles.body: As local agents have moved from experimentation into everyday work, traditional security visibility is no longer enough. Unlike static software, local agents such as coding assistants, command-line agents, desktop applications, and agentic development environments can operate on endpoints with access to a user's data, credentials, tools, and services. They can also connect to Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers that extend their access to additional tools and data. This change requires security teams to look beyond. They need to understand which local agents are running and where, which users and devices these agents are associated with, and which MCP servers these agents are configured to use. To address this challenge, at Microsoft Build 2026, we introduced new Microsoft Defender capabilities to help security teams discover and protect more than 20 types of local AI agents. Today, discovery of AI agents and their configured MCP servers on Windows and macOS is generally available, with discovery coverage expanded to more than 50 supported agents and MCP servers. On eligible, onboarded devices, Defender discovers supported agents by observing their activity and brings the agent, device, account, and configured MCP context together to give security teams visibility for their local agent environment. Beyond discovery, runtime protection for local agents for Windows continues to be available in preview, helping protect discovered agents as they operate. Teams can deploy runtime protection at scale from either the Microsoft Defender portal or the Microsoft Intune portal, with Intune-based deployment available in preview. Both discovery and runtime protection for local agents will be available for Microsoft Defender for Endpoint P2 and higher customers. See the local agents and associated MCPs operating in your environment In the Defender portal, security teams can see the discovered agents under Assets. The inventory associates each agent with the device and user account where it runs and includes details such as agent name, version, vendor, related process, and discovery history. Examples of supported local AI agents include: CLI agents: Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI Desktop applications: ChatGPT Desktop, Claude Desktop, Codex Desktop, GitHub Copilot app, Microsoft Copilot app, Ollama Desktop, Perplexity Desktop Agentic IDEs: Cursor, Devin Desktop, Kiro IDE, Antigravity IDE VS Code extensions: Claude Code, Cline, Codex, Gemini Code...

articles.author: tejaskashyap
articles.body: Linux supports cloud services, containers, developer environments, business-critical applications, and a growing share of AI infrastructure. That makes Linux both essential to modern enterprises and increasingly attractive to attackers. AI is compressing the time required to research targets, vary payloads, and adapt when an attempt fails. Customers need protection that can recognize modern attacker behavior at runtime, continuously test effectiveness against realistic attacks, and learn and evolve with the threat landscape. That’s why Microsoft Defender is focused on three priorities for Linux: stronger runtime protection for fileless and in-memory attacks, continuous validation that proves protection remains effective, and AI-powered defense that can help security teams simulate attacks, investigate threats, close protection gaps, and reduce exploitable paths before compromise. A new Linux threat model The threat landscape has evolved from AI-assisted attacks, where people use AI to accelerate individual tasks, to AI-operated attacks, where AI coordinates more of the attack chain, and now it is moving to autonomous AI attacks that can adapt and act with limited human direction. Modern Linux attacks rarely depend on one file; they combine exposed services, stolen credentials, legitimate administration tools, scripts, containers, and cloud-native attack paths. As AI helps attackers generate and modify payloads at scale, adapt when an attempt fails, and move through the attack chain faster, defenders can no longer assume that every payload, script, or binary will resemble something they have seen before. Microsoft Security Research recently observed compromises involving a LiteLLM gateway, a RAGFlow deployment, and a Kestra workflow environment. The intrusion paths differed, but the objectives converged around credential theft, persistence, downstream access, and compute monetization. The broader lesson is that AI gateways, retrieval platforms, and orchestration services are becoming high-value control points where data, credentials, model connectivity, and workload execution meet. These examples also highlight a broader shift: attackers increasingly abuse legitimate services, tools, and workflows rather than relying solely on overtly malicious binaries. Viewed one event at a time, Bash, Python, curl, SSH, and network connections can appear legitimate. The security challenge is to understand their sequence, process relationships, destinations, and runtime...

The scheduling question Picture four Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) worker nodes with the same hardware. One keeps receiving new batch Jobs even as its CPU usage climbs. But building one that works seamlessly across multiple models and surfaces is incredibly hard. You need to solve for performance, quality, and cost. And then you have to maintain it, which is even harder. Luckily, the GitHub engineering team built a best-in-class, truly multi-model harness, which we’ve adopted company-wide. You get the right model for the job without switching the harness or the rest of your tech stack. That frees up your time, energy, and resources to focus on your bottom line. What’s a harness, and why is it hard? If the model supplies the intelligence, the harness is everything around the model. It’s the orchestration layer that gives an agent the right instructions, context, execution environment, and controls to accomplish meaningful work. And a harness worth its salt has support for open standards like MCP and agent skills, as well as agent plugins. This is a fast-moving space. A frontier model today might fall behind tomorrow. They're ready-to-use templates that turn Defender's email and collaboration data into views your team can use every day, as a Microsoft Sentinel workbook or a Power BI report. Today we're releasing version 4, which builds on Part 3 of this series, with new hunting queries and a new report for attack simulation training. Shaped by customer feedback, it helps you: See the attacks that matter with new Teams and impersonation views. Investigate faster with 125 new or improved hunting queries. Measure and improve resilience with a new attack simulation training report. See the attacks that matter In September, Microsoft Threat Intelligence described a campaign that starts on Teams: an attacker from another organization poses as IT support in a chat or call and talks the user into a remote session. Spotting activity like this early means looking at Teams alongside email. The new Teams & Collaboration view puts those Teams signals in one place: threats in chats and channels, callers and senders with support-style names such as "IT Helpdesk", new external senders, risky links, and the calls and messages users reported. A new Email – Impersonation & BEC tab in the workbook does the same for email, highlighting impersonation attempts that reached an inbox and the people they targeted. Each major workbook tab now opens with key numbers and recommended actions, so the team can go from "what happened?" to "what should we check next?" in one place. In Microsoft Sentinel, the workbook can also combine several workspaces in one view, which helps managed security service providers (MSSPs) and organizations with many tenants. Has this sender contacted us before? Did anyone report a call from them? Are several addresses using the same "IT Helpdesk" display name? articles.author: Microsoft
articles.body: Updated October 26, 2026: We have updated the timeline. Thank you for your patience. [What and why]Users will soon be able to register a passkey as their first multifactor authentication method. Previously, people had to set up an alternate MFA method like SMS or Voice before they could add a passkey (FIDO2), Windows Hello for Business, macOS Platform SSO. That extra step pushed users toward weaker methods and slowed the move to phishing-resistant sign-in. Now password-only users can go straight to a passkey, making it easier to adopt strong authentication from day one. As part of this work, we will also be enabling Authenticator App passwordless sign-in to be a user's first registered MFA method. [Rollout schedule]This feature will roll out in phases: Phase 1: Support for synced passkeys, Microsoft Entra passkeys on Windows, and FIDO2 security keys. General Availability (Worldwide, GCC): We will begin rolling out in early November 2026 (previously late October) and expect to complete by early January 2027 (previously late November 2026). Phase 2: Support for Windows Hello for Business, macOS Platform SSO, Authenticator App passkey, and Authenticator App passwordless sign-in. General Availability (Worldwide, GCC): We will begin rolling out in early January 2026 and expect to complete by late February 2027. [Impact on your organization]Who is affectedUsers who have not yet registered a multifactor authentication methodIdentity and security administrators responsible for authentication onboarding and registration policiesPlatforms and servicesMicrosoft Entra IDPasskeys (FIDO2)Windows Hello for BusinessmacOS Platform SSOMicrosoft Authenticator passwordless sign-inWhat will happenPassword-only users will be able to register passkeys or passwordless sign-in as their first MFA method.Users will no longer need to register a method such as SMS or voice before registering a passkey (FIDO2), Windows Hello for Business, macOS Platform SSO, or Authenticator passwordless sign-in.Organizations may see reduced registration friction and increased adoption of phishing-resistant authentication methods.Users who are enabled for passkeys will be prompted to register a passkey by default when completing applicable registration experiences, including those triggered by multifactor authentication (MFA) enforcement and Conditional Access authentication strengths. Security Defaults MFA registration prompts will adopt this experience in January–February 2027.[Action required and recommendations]No action is required for this change.We recommend that administrators:Review Conditional Access policies related to security information registration.Consider requiring MFA to register security information if additional verification is required by your organization.Review your user onboarding and registration guidance and update it as needed to reflect that eligible users may be prompted to register a passkey by default.Learn more (To be updated closer to rollout) Register a synced passkey (FIDO2) | Authentication | Microsoft Entra ID | Microsoft Learn[Compliance considerations]QuestionAnswerDoes the change include an admin control?Yes. Administrators can control which authentication methods users are allowed to register through existing Microsoft Entra authentication method policies and Conditional Access policies.Does the change affect access or authentication controls?Yes. The update changes how users register multifactor authentication methods by allowing eligible users to register supported passkeys or passwordless authentication methods as their first MFA method.Can administrators govern the feature through existing Microsoft Entra controls?Yes. Administrators retain control over the feature through Microsoft Entra authentication method policies and Conditional Access configurations.

articles.body: Written in collaboration with Gunjan Jain​ and yuvalpery​ As described in our earlier blog, Addressing PHP2Shell CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619: upgrade guidance and Azure WAF mitigations, we strongly recommend upgrading to a patched version of PHP as soon as possible. Upgrading PHP remains the recommended and complete remediation for these vulnerabilities. For customers who are unable to upgrade immediately, this guidance provides WAF custom rules that can help reduce exposure to selected request patterns associated with exploitation techniques for these vulnerabilities. WAF custom rules The following three custom rules can be considered based on your application configuration and traffic patterns. Because custom rules can affect legitimate application traffic, review the potential application impact and validate the rules before enabling enforcement. Restrict PHP session upload progress PHP supports session upload progress for tracking file uploads. For applications that do not depend on this functionality, customers can use a custom rule to restrict multipart form requests containing PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS. The rule checks for multipart/form-data requests whose inspected request body contains the PHP session upload progress token. articles.summary: Email remains the most exploited gateway for cyberattacks, as the threat landscape continues to get more sophisticated with attackers using AI to scale phishing, malware, and business email compromise. Microsoft Defender is a leading email security solution, helping organizations stay ahead of...
articles.author: Oz_Wilder
articles.body: Email remains the most exploited gateway for cyberattacks, as the threat landscape continues to get more sophisticated with attackers using AI to scale phishing, malware, and business email compromise. Microsoft Defender is a leading email security solution, helping organizations stay ahead of these threats with a modern, cloud-native approach. At the same time, many organizations choose to layer additional email security solutions to meet compliance requirements or align to an existing defense-in-depth strategy. This approach can strengthen resilience, but it can also add operational complexity for SOC teams. That’s why one year ago, we introduced the Microsoft Defender Integrated Cloud Email Security (ICES) vendor ecosystem, which is designed to simplify that complexity by integrating partner protections into Microsoft Defender. Today, we’re continuing to expand the ICES vendor ecosystem by adding Proofpoint Core Email Protection API. Proofpoint joins existing members Darktrace, KnowBe4, Cisco, and VIPRE Security Group. How joint customers benefit from a streamlined SOC experience in Microsoft Defender The ICES ecosystem brings trusted third-party email security verdicts and telemetry into the Defender portal through an API-based integration model. This allows Microsoft Defender to acknowledge partner verdicts on messages, apply the highest-severity determination, and surface that information in the same investigation and response workflows security teams already use. The integration with Proofpoint Core Email Protection API is designed specifically for customers who have already chosen to deploy Proofpoint’s ICES solution alongside Microsoft Defender. It supports environments where customers run both solutions and want to reduce friction for their SOC teams. By integrating Proofpoint into the ICES ecosystem, customers can now preserve their existing security strategy while improving how investigations and response are carried out day to day. "Organizations rely on both Microsoft and Proofpoint to protect their most critical communications and data. By extending Proofpoint’s interoperability across ICES, we’re delivering a more unified security experience that strengthens defense-in-depth and simplifies operations for our shared customers. This milestone reflects our commitment to joint customers worldwide.” - Tom Corn, EVP and GM, Threat Protection Group at Proofpoint Below we have outlined how Proofpoint’s ICES solution now integrates within Microsoft...

articles.author: Amy Coleman
articles.body: Amy Coleman, Executive Vice President and Chief People Officer, shared the below communication with Microsoft employees today. Today, we’re introducing a new Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) to eligible employees within participating organizations. This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support. It also gives participating organizations another way to adapt their workforce to changing needs. The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we’re evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter. This builds on what we learned earlier this year through the Voluntary Retirement Program. What employees should know This offer will be available to eligible employees in participating teams in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the United States at level 70 and below. This is a time-limited, voluntary program that gives those who are eligible the opportunity to leave Microsoft with financial support and career planning resources. Some organizations are providing the Voluntary Exit Offer, and some are not. Participation varies based on each business’s priorities, customer commitments and workforce needs. Eligible employees will receive an email with a link to their Voluntary Exit Offer details within the next few hours. Looking ahead The Voluntary Exit Offer is new for us. We’ll learn from it. At the same time, we’ll keep helping people focus on the work that matters most, build new skills and, where it makes sense, find new opportunities across Microsoft. There is no one-size-fits-all approach for every team or every employee. These are a few of the ways we’re trying to meet different business needs while continuing to create opportunities for our own people to grow and contribute. My promise is to continue to provide clarity, listen and learn and keep improving. Thank you for everything you continue to do for our customers, Microsoft and for one another.
